view: Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad is reported to read mā qarabtum, 'what you brought near,' and a related report gives 'what you bring near for them' in place of 'what you laid up'; the latter is glossed as placing the harvest near in the revealed sequence.
note: The reported variants concern wording outside the quoted verse.

view: The messenger's 'the people' can mean the king and his people, or respectfully refer to the king alone.
note: This concerns the preceding request to return to the people.

view: Qatada reports that Joseph left home at seventeen, spent seven years in the well and seven in prison, stored food for seven years, and, according to the report's audience, then met his father.
A Prophetic report marvels at Joseph's patience and generosity: though asked to interpret the cows, he did not hurry out when summoned and wanted his innocence established.
Joseph served one man food for two, leaving half uneaten each day; when the man consumed the whole serving, Joseph recognized that the first hard year had begun.

A report from al-Riḍā says Joseph stockpiled harvests and sold famine food successively for money, valuables, livestock, servants, property, land, and freedom, then freed Egyptians and restored their possessions and kingship.
The commentator omits many similar accounts of the famine economy because most do not directly aid interpretation of these verses.

The dream calls for a practical famine policy of repeated planting, preserving grain in its ears, and rationing reserves; it is not merely a forecast of seven fertile years followed by seven barren ones.
note: This disputes the reading that takes Joseph's words chiefly as a forecast of the sequence of years.

view: Joseph added practical advice on cultivation, storage, and provisioning to his interpretation of the dream; his answer also conveys a later unseen year.
note: Ibn Ashur calls the king's dream divine kindness to Egypt and perhaps a sign of the king's readiness for faith and reform; Abu Hayyan distinguishes interpretation, advice, and the unseen report.

view: One account says Joseph knew the additional abundant year through direct revelation, beyond dream interpretation; another says God had taught him the interpretation, so his forecast was certain.
note: The positions disagree over direct revelation versus knowledge taught for dream interpretation; Qatada says God granted Joseph knowledge of the later year.

view: Joseph may have omitted an audible 'if God wills' while intending the exception inwardly, just as his brothers did when promising to bring their brother.
note: Offered as an answer to why the prediction lacks an explicit exception.

view: The messenger's hope that 'they may know' expresses concern that a false dream or rejection might prevent acceptance until events confirm the interpretation; it does not express doubt in Joseph.
note: This concerns the preceding request and its outcome.

view: Revealed laws guide worldly interests so people may know and worship God and attain happiness after death; according to Sunni authorities, this care is divine grace, not an obligation God owes.
Preserving public interests serves religion, life, intellect, lineage, and property; safeguarding these is benefit, their loss is harm, and averting harm is itself benefit.

The Qur'anic account of Joseph illustrates God's hidden direction of human affairs, in which people may dislike what benefits them or love what harms them, as in 2:216; this differs from Genesis' romantic account of his fortunes.
Ḥarth denotes sowing seed and preparing the soil, while zarʿ denotes tending and growing a crop and may also include sowing; God causes its growth.
The imperative to leave the grain can follow a declarative prediction: it may be independent advice, an answer to an implied condition, or guidance expressed in the form of a report.
note: These are replies to the objection that an imperative cannot be coordinated with a declarative forecast.

view: The declarative 'you cultivate' functions as a command to sow; expressing the command as a report emphasizes compliance or presents the action as certain. The following explicit command to leave the harvest in its ears supports this reading.
note: Mawardi adds that Joseph as a prophet may advise people on their interests; Ibn al-Jawzi offers this command reading as one answer to why Joseph did not say 'if God wills'.

view: A present verb can also express a prayer; because prayer asks for an act, this use resembles an imperative, as illustrated by the plea to forgive and show mercy in 23:118.
'You cultivate' predicts seven successive years of ordinary farming; the later command to store grain supplies new advice and does not turn the prediction into an imperative.
note: Abu Hayyan adds irrigation. Al-Samin says routine farming needed no instruction, whereas preservation did; al-Kashf says the storage advice interrupts the forecast with urgency. This disputes the command reading.

view: Daʾban can instead qualify the seven years themselves as continuous.
note: This differs from taking it as a state of the cultivators.

view: The seven fat cows and green ears signify seven fertile years, and the lean cows and dry ears seven years of famine or drought; the cultivation years supply the food later needed.
note: Ibn Kathir adds that cows symbolize years because they plow fields, and describes the fertile years as rainy; Ibn Ashur takes ears as provisions. Al-Qummi's reported account adds rain after the famine.

view: In the dream's imagery, cows represent yearly provisions: fat cows show plentiful harvests from sustained planting, lean cows shortages, and the lean cows eating the fat ones famine consuming saved food.
note: Part of the practical-policy reading of the dream.

view: Each of the seven green ears stands for one year's food, signifying seven years whose harvest is eaten fresh.
Joseph's answer concerns a fifteen-year agricultural cycle: seven productive years, seven years of scarcity, and a further abundant year.
note: The further year is connected with revelation in the cited notes.

view: The phrase can mean seven consecutive years of planting, year after year, following the people's established agricultural practice.
note: Ibn Abbas especially glosses it as consecutive years.

view: Daʾb denotes a habitual or customary practice, here the usual course of farming; the cited verse of Imru al-Qays uses it for customary conduct toward Umm al-Huwayrith and her neighbor, and another line uses ka-daʾbika.
note: Some of these notes also give the related senses of persistence and toil.

view: Daʾb also means sustained, diligent effort or perseverance: they keep working at cultivation. Its root is illustrated by al-Kumayt's persistent travel, and al-Raghib extends continued travel to lasting habitual practice.
note: The notes variously stress customary conduct, continuous work, and strenuous effort.

view: One distinction treats the form with sukūn as a verbal noun and the form with fatḥa as a noun; others treat both pronunciations as verbal nouns of persistent work.
note: The notes disagree about whether the vowel marks a difference in grammatical category.

view: Daʾban is an accusative verbal noun governed by an omitted verb of its own root, 'you persevere'; the labor implied by 'you cultivate' supplies its meaning.
note: Associated with Sibawayh, al-Farraʾ, al-Zajjaj, and Abu Ali in different notes; the implied verb is indicated by the sense of sowing.

view: Al-Mubarrad attaches daʾban directly to 'you cultivate' as an accusative of manner or absolute object because cultivation implies diligent work; al-Samin and al-Alusi object that it is not a particular manner of sowing comparable to the cited manner of sitting.
note: The dispute turns on whether the verb of cultivation can govern this verbal noun without an omitted verb.

view: Daʾban may be a verbal noun used adverbially or as a circumstantial accusative describing the cultivators as working persistently; proposed analyses include an intensive noun, adjective position, an omitted 'diligent people,' or metaphorical identity.
note: The circumstantial and adverbial descriptions share the sense of persistence, but the listed grammatical explanations differ.

view: Most listed readers, including Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, al-Kisaʾi and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, read the hamza with sukūn; Hafs from ʿAsim reads it with fatḥa, and a fatḥa transmission from ʿAsim is also recorded. Both forms convey persistent work.
note: Musa al-Zabi also reports ʿAsim's fatḥa; the majority's still hamza and Hafs's open hamza are described as valid forms.

view: Abu ʿAmr drops or eases the hamza in connected recitation; another variant removes it altogether as a phonological simplification.
At a pause the form is dābā; recitation resumes with daʾban.
Abu Hatim reports Yaʿqub reading the hamza with a vowel and deriving the form from daʾiba; al-Naḥḥās objects that Arab linguists recognize only daʾb.
note: The dispute concerns whether the proposed derivation is attested in Arabic.

view: The still hamza is the commoner form; fatḥa may be a dialectal variant, like the cited variants in shamʿ and nahr, or arise from easing a guttural consonant. Kufans permit such vowel changes generally, while Basrans require attested usage.
note: Al-Farraʾ's rule concerns gutturals, including hamza; the Kufan and Basran positions differ over analogy beyond heard forms.

view: Sukūn is preferred because the same word is consistently read that way in the expression about Pharaoh's people.
note: This is a preference among the recited forms, tied to 8:54.

view: The expression daʾb is also discussed in connection with its occurrence at 3:11.
Mā in 'what you harvest' may be either conditional or a relative pronoun.
Joseph sought to preserve the harvest and build food reserves for the coming scarcity.
note: Qatada explicitly says the advice aimed at reserves.

view: 'Leave it' is explicitly imperative, although the preceding cultivation clause has declarative form; the verbs dhar and daʿ lack past-tense forms because taraka supplies that function.
note: The unusual verb paradigm is reported separately from the contrast in clause forms.

view: If 'you cultivate' is read as an imperative, the storage command may be part of interpreting the dream because the lean cows and dry ears anticipate eating earlier produce, or it may be advice outside the interpretation.
note: The two positions differ on whether the storage instruction belongs to dream interpretation.

view: Leave most harvested grain unthreshed in its ears or husk: it keeps longer and remains sound, protected from weevils, termites, insects, and spoilage.
note: Several notes describe Egyptian wheat as especially vulnerable and specify that insects attack threshed or piled grain.

view: The dream's green ears may have suggested Joseph's unusual advice to store grain in its ears.
The dream's green ears depict stores that must be saved and its dry ears point to keeping grain unthreshed; the imagery indicates the work needed to protect supplies.
note: Part of the practical-policy reading of the dream.

view: Egyptian grain may fail to keep for even two years outside its ear, so storage in the ear is especially useful there; consume the oldest stored grain first while retaining the rest for famine.
note: Al-Alusi describes such stores as liable to ruin after roughly two years.

view: Grain left in its ear is not readily eaten, which helps preserve the stockpile.
Thresh or draw out only the little grain needed for food during the seven productive years; eat sparingly and store the rest for the barren years.
note: Bursevi and al-Alusi explicitly draw the lesson of restraint or moderation.

view: The exception permits the people to use enough for food during the productive years; it is a permission rather than part of dream interpretation.
Seed grain need not be separately excepted from the stored harvest because the instruction to keep cultivating already implies saving seed.
note: Kuranyolu explicitly mentions setting aside both food and seed.

view: Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, also named al-Sulamī, reads 'what they eat' with third-person yā, referring to the people; it may also be understood as a shift of address.
